claim: In human small and large intestines, expression of SOX10 and PLP1 was restricted to a cluster of cells with a glial signature.
source: In human small and large intestines, expression of SOX10 and PLP1 was restricted to cluster of cells with a glial signature (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of publicly available scRNAseq datasets shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: S100B was highly expressed by cells in the glial cluster but also detected in non-glial cells including macrophages and monocytes in human intestinal mucosa.
source: S100B was highly expressed by cells in this cluster but also detected in non-glial cells including macrophages and monocytes; GFAP was overall undetectable (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: GFAP was overall undetectable in human intestinal mucosal glia by scRNAseq.
source: S100B was highly expressed by cells in this cluster but also detected in non-glial cells including macrophages and monocytes; GFAP was overall undetectable (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: SOX10-, PLP1-, and S100B-immunoreactive cells were found in the mucosa, enteric ganglia in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses, and intramuscular glia in the muscularis externa of human small intestine.
source: To validate these findings, we examined expression of the corresponding proteins by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in the human small intestine and found SOX10-, PLP1-, and S100B-immunoreactive cells in three compartments along the radial axis: the mucosa, enteric ganglia in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses, as well as intramuscular glia in the muscularis externa (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFAP-immunoreactive cells were readily found within enteric ganglia but were rare in the mucosa of human small intestine.
source: GFAP-immunoreactive cells were readily found within enteric ganglia but were rare in the mucosa (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A recent study examined SOX10, GFAP, and S100B by IHC in the human colon and found little to no GFAP, but robust SOX10 and S100B expression across all three compartments.
source: These observations are consistent with a recent study that examined SOX10, GFAP, and S100B by IHC in the human colon and found little to no GFAP, but robust SOX10 and S100B expression across all three compartments (Baidoo et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: In the small intestine of patients with Crohn's disease, SOX10, PLP1, and S100B transcripts were highly enriched in mucosal glia while GFAP was enriched in various non-glial cells including fibroblasts and immune cells.
source: In the small intestine of patients with Crohn's disease, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), SOX10, PLP1, and S100B transcripts were highly enriched in mucosal glia while GFAP was enriched in various non-glial cells including fibroblasts and immune cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SOX10, PLP1, and S100B are broadly expressed by human enteric glia across the radial axis of the gut, including mucosal glia, in both healthy and inflamed states.
source: In sum, SOX10, PLP1, and S100B are broadly expressed by human enteric glia across the radial axis of the gut, including mucosal glia, in both healthy and inflamed states, with SOX10 and PLP1 exhibiting the most cell type specificity.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on multiple data sources presented in the manuscript.

claim: SOX10 and PLP1 exhibit the most cell type specificity among glial markers in human intestine.
source: In sum, SOX10, PLP1, and S100B are broadly expressed by human enteric glia across the radial axis of the gut, including mucosal glia, in both healthy and inflamed states, with SOX10 and PLP1 exhibiting the most cell type specificity.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on multiple data sources presented in the manuscript.

claim: PLP1 is widely expressed by enteric glia across the radial axis of the mouse small and large intestines where its expression largely overlaps with S100B.
source: In mice, we previously showed that PLP1 is widely expressed by enteric glia across the radial axis of the small and large intestines where its expression largely overlaps with S100B; a more limited subset expresses GFAP (Rao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: A more limited subset of mouse enteric glia expresses GFAP compared to PLP1 and S100B.
source: In mice, we previously showed that PLP1 is widely expressed by enteric glia across the radial axis of the small and large intestines where its expression largely overlaps with S100B; a more limited subset expresses GFAP (Rao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Plp1 is broadly expressed across the single putative cluster of mucosal glia in mouse colonic mucosa by scRNAseq.
source: Consistent with these observations, analysis of scRNAseq data from the mouse colonic mucosa showed that Plp1 is broadly expressed across the single putative cluster of mucosal glia; Gfap, S100b, and Sox10 are also detectable in this cluster to variable extents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Gfap, S100b, and Sox10 are detectable in the putative cluster of mucosal glia in mouse colonic mucosa to variable extents.
source: Consistent with these observations, analysis of scRNAseq data from the mouse colonic mucosa showed that Plp1 is broadly expressed across the single putative cluster of mucosal glia; Gfap, S100b, and Sox10 are also detectable in this cluster to variable extents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A subset of Gfaphigh/Plp1low mucosal glia might be particularly important for epithelial regulation in the mouse small intestine.
source: Given recent observations that a subset of Gfaphigh/Plp1low mucosal glia might be particularly important for epithelial regulation in the mouse small intestine (Baghdadi et al., 2022), we closely compared Plp1 and Gfap expression in the mouse ileum.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: eGFP expression in Plp1-eGFP reporter mice faithfully mirrors endogenous PLP1 expression within the enteric and central nervous systems.
source: Previous work from our lab and others has validated that eGFP expression in this reporter strain faithfully mirrors endogenous PLP1 expression within the enteric and central nervous systems (Rao et al., 2015; Mallon et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The majority of villus Plp1+ cells co-expressed GFAP in adult mouse ileum.
source: In adult Plp1-eGFP mice, we found that mucosal glia diverged sharply in terms of marker expression based on their location along the crypt-villus axis. While the majority of villus Plp1+ cells co-expressed GFAP, virtually none of the crypt-associated Plp1+ cells did so (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Virtually none of the crypt-associated Plp1+ cells co-expressed GFAP in adult mouse ileum.
source: In adult Plp1-eGFP mice, we found that mucosal glia diverged sharply in terms of marker expression based on their location along the crypt-villus axis. While the majority of villus Plp1+ cells co-expressed GFAP, virtually none of the crypt-associated Plp1+ cells did so (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: GFAP-immunoreactive cells that did not express Plp1 were largely undetectable in mouse ileum with rare exceptions in some villi.
source: With rare exceptions in some villi, GFAP-immunoreactive cells that did not express Plp1 were largely undetectable.
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry observations.

claim: Plp1 expression broadly marks enteric glia in mouse and human tissues.
source: Together, these observations indicate that Plp1 expression broadly marks enteric glia in mouse and human tissues and is among the most sensitive and specific markers for glia in the gut mucosa.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on multiple data sources presented in the manuscript.

claim: Plp1 is among the most sensitive and specific markers for glia in the gut mucosa.
source: Together, these observations indicate that Plp1 expression broadly marks enteric glia in mouse and human tissues and is among the most sensitive and specific markers for glia in the gut mucosa.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on multiple data sources presented in the manuscript.

claim: Plp1CreER Rosa26DTA/+ mice exhibit loss of the majority of S100B- and SOX10-expressing enteric glia, including 90% of mucosal glia.
source: We depleted the cells by administration of tamoxifen to young adult Plp1CreER Rosa26DTA/+ mice, which we previously showed exhibit loss of the majority of S100B- and SOX10-expressing enteric glia, including 90% of mucosal glia (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: In the Plp1CreER Rosa26DTA/+ model, glia are lost within 5 days of tamoxifen induction (5dpt) and remain stably depleted through 14dpt.
source: In this model, glia are lost within 5 days of tamoxifen induction (5dpt) and remain stably depleted through 14dpt; notably female, but not male, mice have intestinal dysmotility (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Female, but not male, Plp1CreER Rosa26DTA/+ mice have intestinal dysmotility.
source: In this model, glia are lost within 5 days of tamoxifen induction (5dpt) and remain stably depleted through 14dpt; notably female, but not male, mice have intestinal dysmotility (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: There were minimal changes in the transcriptome in the duodenum and ileum of glial-ablated mice at 11dpt.
source: Surprisingly, there were minimal changes observed in the transcriptome in all three regions of the intestine though the mice exhibited robust depletion of S100B+ glia by IHC. In the duodenum and ileum, differential gene expression analysis by DESeq2 revealed no genes that reached the standard threshold for statistical significance of padj <0.05 (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: In the colon, only five genes were differentially expressed upon glial ablation, most of which were upregulated in glial-ablated mice.
source: In the colon, only five genes were differentially expressed, most of which were upregulated in glial-ablated mice (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: Acute depletion of enteric glia in male mice has limited effects on the intestinal transcriptome.
source: These results suggest that acute depletion of enteric glia in male mice has limited effects on the intestinal transcriptome.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the RNA-seq data presented.

claim: Most genes that were differentially expressed upon glial depletion were highly specific to one region of the intestine.
source: Most genes that were differentially expressed were highly specific to one region of the intestine (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DiVenn analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 331, 516, and 916 genes were changed uniquely in duodenum, ileum, and colon, respectively, upon glial depletion.
source: While 331, 516, and 916 genes were changed uniquely in duodenum, ileum, and colon, respectively, only 16–29 genes were shared between pairs of tissues (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DiVenn analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only 16–29 genes were shared between pairs of tissues (duodenum, ileum, colon) upon glial depletion.
source: While 331, 516, and 916 genes were changed uniquely in duodenum, ileum, and colon, respectively, only 16–29 genes were shared between pairs of tissues (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DiVenn analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only two genes (Igkv4-91 and Ighv1-58) were differentially expressed between Cre- and Cre+ mice in all three tissue regions (duodenum, ileum, colon).
source: Remarkably, only two genes were differentially expressed between Cre- and Cre+ mice in all three tissue regions (Igkv4-91 and Ighv1-58), suggesting that enteric glia exert region-specific effects along the longitudinal axis of the intestine.
evidence: The claim is supported by DiVenn analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Enteric glia exert region-specific effects along the longitudinal axis of the intestine.
source: Remarkably, only two genes were differentially expressed between Cre- and Cre+ mice in all three tissue regions (Igkv4-91 and Ighv1-58), suggesting that enteric glia exert region-specific effects along the longitudinal axis of the intestine.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the DiVenn analysis data.

claim: Lyz1 was the top gene upregulated in the colons of Cre+ mice.
source: Focusing on the colon, which showed the most evidence of altered gene expression upon glial loss, we examined the expression of Lyz1, the top gene upregulated in Cre+ mice (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: LYZ1 is an antimicrobial peptide that is highly and relatively specifically expressed by Paneth cells in the small intestine.
source: LYZ1 is an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) that is highly and relatively specifically expressed by Paneth cells in the small intestine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Peeters and Vantrappen, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and citation to a published study.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR of colonic tissue confirmed upregulation of Lyz1 in the colons of Cre+ mice.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR (qPCR) of colonic tissue isolated from independent cohorts of Plp1CreER Rosa26DTA/+ mice confirmed upregulation of Lyz1 in the colons of Cre+ mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Reactome pathway analysis of differentially enriched genes in the colon highlighted pathways characteristic of Paneth cells including defensins and other AMPs.
source: Reactome pathway analysis of differentially enriched genes in the colon also highlighted pathways characteristic of Paneth cells including defensins and other AMPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Reactome pathway analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Paneth cells are not typically present in the healthy mouse colon.
source: Paneth cells are not typically present in the healthy mouse colon and their ectopic appearance is considered a marker of inflammation (Hertzog, 1937; Paterson and Watson, 1961; Tanaka et al., 2001; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Ectopic appearance of Paneth cells in the mouse colon is considered a marker of inflammation.
source: Paneth cells are not typically present in the healthy mouse colon and their ectopic appearance is considered a marker of inflammation (Hertzog, 1937; Paterson and Watson, 1961; Tanaka et al., 2001; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: No LYZ1- or DEFA5-immunoreactive epithelial cells were detected in the colons of either Cre- or Cre+ mice.
source: Although both markers robustly labeled Paneth cells in the small intestine, no LYZ1- or DEFA5-immunoreactive epithelial cells were detected in the colons of either Cre- or Cre+ mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Acute glial depletion causes transcriptional dysregulation in the colon linked to Paneth cell biology without evidence of ectopic Paneth cells or corresponding changes in proteins.
source: These data suggest that acute glial depletion causes transcriptional dysregulation in the colon linked to Paneth cell biology without evidence of ectopic Paneth cells or corresponding changes in proteins.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry data presented.

claim: Glia might be most important for epithelial homeostasis in the ileum.
source: Previous studies have indicated that glia might be most important for epithelial homeostasis in the ileum (Bush et al., 1998; Cornet et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: There was minimal overlap in the transcriptional changes observed in the whole ileum compared to the ileal epithelium upon glial depletion.
source: DESeq2 and DiVenn analysis detected minimal overlap in the transcriptional changes observed in the whole ileum compared to the ileal epithelium, supporting the utility of focused epithelial analysis (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by DESeq2 and DiVenn analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No genes reached the padj <0.05 threshold of significance for differential expression in the ileal epithelium upon glial depletion.
source: Most intestinal epithelial cells turn over every 3–5 days (Darwich et al., 2014) and thus the majority of cells represented in the epithelial transcriptome of Cre+ mice would not have experienced glial interactions. Nevertheless, epithelial gene expression was similar in control and glial-ablated mice, mirroring the findings from whole tissue. No genes reached the padj <0.05 threshold of significance for differential expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Most intestinal epithelial cells turn over every 3–5 days.
source: Most intestinal epithelial cells turn over every 3–5 days (Darwich et al., 2014) and thus the majority of cells represented in the epithelial transcriptome of Cre+ mice would not have experienced glial interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: The Paneth cell signature was most significantly enriched in the ileal epithelium of glia-depleted mice by GSEA.
source: To determine if glial depletion selectively affected any of these cell types, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using cell-type-specific signatures obtained from a published scRNAseq study (Haber et al., 2017; Supplementary file 1). Several of these signatures, most significantly that of Paneth cells (p<0.001, FDR <0.001), were enriched in the transcriptional profile of Cre+ mice (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: An independent GSEA using curated cell signatures derived from bulk RNASeq studies showed an enrichment of the Paneth cell program in glial-depleted mice.
source: An independent GSEA using curated cell signatures derived from bulk RNASeq studies also showed an enrichment of the Paneth cell program (p<0.001, FDR <0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Immunostaining revealed no difference in the densities of Paneth, Lgr5+, goblet, enteroendocrine, and microfold (M) cells in Cre+ mice compared to Cre- littermates.
source: Immunostaining for molecular markers of Paneth, Lgr5+, goblet, enteroendocrine, and microfold (M) cells, however, revealed no difference in their densities in Cre+ mice compared to Cre- littermates (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C–D.

claim: In glial-ablated mice, all epithelial cell types appeared grossly normal, except for Paneth cells.
source: In glial-ablated mice, all these cell types also appeared grossly normal, except for Paneth cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Paneth cells are highly secretory cells located at the crypt base that are responsible for production and release of the bulk of small intestinal AMPs.
source: Paneth cells are highly secretory cells located at the crypt base that are responsible for production and release of the bulk of small intestinal AMPs, such as LYZ1 and α-defensins, which are crucial for homeostatic regulation of the microbiome and innate immunity (Peeters and Vantrappen, 1975; Jones and Bevins, 1992; Salzman et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 1999; Salzman et al., 2010; Clevers and Bevins, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: LYZ1 and α-defensins are crucial for homeostatic regulation of the microbiome and innate immunity.
source: Paneth cells are highly secretory cells located at the crypt base that are responsible for production and release of the bulk of small intestinal AMPs, such as LYZ1 and α-defensins, which are crucial for homeostatic regulation of the microbiome and innate immunity (Peeters and Vantrappen, 1975; Jones and Bevins, 1992; Salzman et al., 2003; Wilson et al., 1999; Salzman et al., 2010; Clevers and Bevins, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Many Paneth cells in Cre+ mice had heterogenous secretory granules, some of which appeared giant, fused, or dysmorphic.
source: Labeling Paneth cell granules with the fucose-specific lectin UEA-1, revealed that many Paneth cells in Cre+ mice had heterogenous secretory granules, some of which appeared giant, fused, or dysmorphic (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Paneth cells in Cre- mice had typical morphology with a pyramidal shape, extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum, and relatively homogenous, electron-dense granules with haloes, which were oriented toward the apical surface of the cell.
source: On ultrastructural analysis by transmission electron microscopy, Paneth cells in Cre- mice had typical morphology with a pyramidal shape, extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum, and relatively homogenous, electron-dense granules with haloes, which were oriented toward the apical surface of the cell (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Cre+ mice, Paneth cells had normal rough endoplasmic reticulum, but many exhibited a globular morphology and contained more heterogeneous granules.
source: In Cre+ mice, Paneth cells had normal rough endoplasmic reticulum, but many exhibited a globular morphology and contained more heterogeneous granules (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neighboring intestinal stem cells in the crypt base, as well as other secretory cell types such as enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells appeared no different in Cre- and Cre+ mice.
source: In contrast, neighboring intestinal stem cells in the crypt base, as well as other secretory cell types such as enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells appeared no different in Cre- and Cre+ mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glial depletion did not provoke major shifts in small intestinal epithelial gene expression or cell composition but caused upregulation of Paneth cell genes associated with specific morphological changes that were highly specific to this cell type.
source: In sum, glial depletion did not provoke major shifts in small intestinal epithelial gene expression or cell composition but caused upregulation of Paneth cell genes associated with specific morphological changes that were highly specific to this cell type.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on multiple data sources presented in the manuscript.

claim: Paneth cells secrete their granules both constitutively and in response to various stimuli, such as pathogen-associated molecular patterns and cholinergic agonists.
source: Paneth cells secrete their granules both constitutively and in response to various stimuli, such as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (Ayabe et al., 2000) and cholinergic agonists (Satoh et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: At the level of individual cells, disruption of Paneth cell secretory activity can manifest as accumulation and/or fusion of their secretory granules.
source: At the level of individual cells, disruption of this secretory activity can manifest as accumulation and/or fusion of their secretory granules (Satoh, 1988; Ahonen, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The abnormal granule appearance in Cre+ mice suggested that glial depletion might compromise Paneth cell secretion.
source: The abnormal granule appearance in Cre+ mice suggested that glial depletion might compromise Paneth cell secretion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the morphological observations.

claim: The 'extracellular' and 'secretory' cellular compartments were most enriched in pathway analysis of Paneth cell genes that were changed in glial-depleted mice.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the 'extracellular' and 'secretory' cellular compartments were most enriched in pathway analysis of Paneth cell genes that were changed in glial-depleted mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Pre-treatment of mice with dithizone, a zinc chelator known to selectively deplete Paneth cell granules, reduced detectable lysozyme activity in the explant assay.
source: Supporting this assay's specificity for Paneth cell-derived lysozyme, pre-treatment of mice with dithizone, a zinc chelator known to selectively deplete Paneth cell granules (Sawada et al., 1991; Lueschow et al., 2018), reduced detectable lysozyme activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by lysozyme activity assay data shown in Figure 5C and citations to published studies.

claim: Small intestinal explants from Cre+ mice secreted less active lysozyme than those from Cre- controls.
source: Utilizing this assay, we found that small intestinal explants from Cre+ mice secreted less active lysozyme than those from Cre- controls (Figure 5C), indicating that glial loss disrupts Paneth cell secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by lysozyme activity assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Glial loss disrupts Paneth cell secretion.
source: Utilizing this assay, we found that small intestinal explants from Cre+ mice secreted less active lysozyme than those from Cre- controls (Figure 5C), indicating that glial loss disrupts Paneth cell secretion.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lysozyme activity assay data.

claim: Cholinergic signaling regulates Paneth cell function.
source: Cholinergic signaling regulates Paneth cell function (Satoh et al., 1989; Satoh, 1988; Satoh et al., 1992; Satoh et al., 1995; Dolan et al., 2022) and genetic depletion of G proteins that act downstream of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) alters granule morphology (Watanabe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Genetic depletion of G proteins that act downstream of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors alters Paneth cell granule morphology.
source: Cholinergic signaling regulates Paneth cell function (Satoh et al., 1989; Satoh, 1988; Satoh et al., 1992; Satoh et al., 1995; Dolan et al., 2022) and genetic depletion of G proteins that act downstream of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) alters granule morphology (Watanabe et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 3 (mAChR3) is the major neurotransmitter receptor expressed by Paneth cells.
source: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 3 (mAChR3) is the major neurotransmitter receptor expressed by Paneth cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B; Dolan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and citation to a published study.

claim: mAChR3 expression level in the epithelium was unchanged by glial loss.
source: Its expression level in the epithelium was unchanged by glial loss (log2FC = 0.104762356, p-value = 0.6474, padj = 0.9999).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Paneth cells in Cre+ mice remained capable of degranulation in response to the cholinergic agonist, carbachol.
source: In line with this observation, Paneth cells in Cre+ mice remained capable of degranulation in response to the cholinergic agonist, carbachol, and secreted similar levels of lysozyme upon carbachol stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Paneth cells in Cre+ mice secreted similar levels of lysozyme upon carbachol stimulation compared to Cre- mice.
source: In line with this observation, Paneth cells in Cre+ mice remained capable of degranulation in response to the cholinergic agonist, carbachol, and secreted similar levels of lysozyme upon carbachol stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Paneth cells in mice lacking enteric glia exhibit morphological and functional evidence of diminished secretory function at baseline but remain competent to respond to at least some stimuli.
source: Thus, Paneth cells in mice lacking enteric glia exhibit morphological and functional evidence of diminished secretory function at baseline but remain competent to respond to at least some stimuli.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on multiple data sources presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the skin, glia are essential for the maintenance of nerve terminals, and glial depletion causes rapid and dramatic denervation.
source: In the skin, another critical barrier tissue, glia are essential for the maintenance of nerve terminals, and glial depletion causes rapid and dramatic denervation (Li and Ginty, 2014; Rinwa et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The density of crypt innervation was no different between Cre+ and Cre- mice.
source: To determine if enteric glial depletion similarly causes intestinal epithelial denervation that might result in decreased Paneth cell stimulation, we characterized crypt-associated neuronal fibers in Cre+ and Cre- mice. Overall, the density of crypt innervation was no different in the two groups of mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Most nerve fibers surrounding crypts are from cholinergic neurons and these fibers tightly associate with enteric glia.
source: Many types of intrinsic and extrinsic neurons innervate the intestinal epithelium. We found that most nerve fibers surrounding crypts are from cholinergic neurons and these fibers tightly associate with enteric glia (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are among the few neurotransmitter receptors expressed by Paneth cells.
source: Given that muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are among the few neurotransmitter receptors expressed by Paneth cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B; Dolan et al., 2022), cholinergic neurons are likely the ones most relevant to Paneth cell function.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and citation to a published study.

claim: Cholinergic neurons are likely the ones most relevant to Paneth cell function.
source: Given that muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are among the few neurotransmitter receptors expressed by Paneth cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B; Dolan et al., 2022), cholinergic neurons are likely the ones most relevant to Paneth cell function.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the receptor expression data.

claim: There was no difference in the presentation of cholinergic nerve terminals that surround epithelial crypts between Cre- and Cre+ mice.
source: To test whether these neurons are altered by glial depletion, we assessed vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) immunoreactivity in Cre- and Cre+ mice. We observed no difference in the presentation of cholinergic nerve terminals that surround epithelial crypts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Glia are not required to maintain epithelial innervation in the intestine.
source: These observations establish that glia are not required to maintain epithelial innervation in the intestine and that Paneth cell defects in glial-depleted mice do not result from loss of cholinergic innervation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the innervation data presented.

claim: Paneth cell defects in glial-depleted mice do not result from loss of cholinergic innervation.
source: These observations establish that glia are not required to maintain epithelial innervation in the intestine and that Paneth cell defects in glial-depleted mice do not result from loss of cholinergic innervation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the innervation data presented.

claim: Paneth-cell-derived antimicrobial peptides are essential for preventing microbial colonization of intestinal crypts in the small intestine.
source: Paneth-cell-derived antimicrobial peptides are essential for preventing microbial colonization of intestinal crypts in the small intestine (Meyer-Hoffert et al., 2008; Vaishnava et al., 2011) and modulating the overall structure of the gut microbiome (Salzman et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Paneth-cell-derived antimicrobial peptides modulate the overall structure of the gut microbiome.

claim: Previous studies reached conflicting conclusions about whether glial-epithelial interactions are important in vivo.
source: Glial cells of the enteric nervous system (ENS) interact closely with the intestinal epithelium and secrete signals that influence epithelial cell proliferation and barrier formation in vitro. Whether these interactions are important in vivo, however, is unclear because previous studies reached conflicting conclusions (Prochera and Rao, 2023).
